data.title: Pohanská – a Celtic oppidum above Plavecké Podhradie
data.excerpt: Pohanská rises on spot height 497 on the western slope of the Lesser Carpathians, in the cadastral area of Plavecké Podhradie, with the ruin of the medieval castle known as Plavecký zámok 550 m to the north. In the Late La Tène period it became a Celtic oppidum of 49 hectares behind three rings of ramparts – perhaps one of the largest enclosed prehistoric settlements in Slovakia – and it was destroyed by fire in the first half of the 1st century BC.
data.metaTitle: Pohanská – a Celtic oppidum at Plavecké Podhradie
data.metaDescription: The Celtic oppidum of Pohanská (497 m) in the Lesser Carpathians: 49 ha behind three rings of ramparts, destroyed by fire in the 1st century BC.

children.text: Pohanská rises on spot height 497 on the western slope of the Lesser Carpathians, in the cadastral area of the village of Plavecké Podhradie. To the north of it, at a distance of 550 m, stands the ruin of the medieval castle known as Plavecký zámok. At this point Pohanská forms the foothills, and a considerably high one at that, since the highest summits of the central belt of the Lesser Carpathians, which runs to the east of it, rise barely 60 m above it. The view of Pohanská from the north and the west – as of a mountain emerging suddenly from a monotonous plain – is therefore beautiful, even captivating. In good visibility, too, the eye can take in from its summit a wide horizon from Javorina in the north-west, the outlines of the White Carpathians, the Buchlov hills above Velehrad, the Pálava hills in southern Moravia and, to the south, as far as the Vienna Woods. These circumstances certainly played an important part in the choice of the place as a refuge for the population and its property, and as an extensive fortified seat of tribal administration, both civil and religious. As Štefan Janšák already wrote,

today one cannot look out from the summit of Pohanská without emotion. And what must primitive man have felt, who explained everything by supernatural forces – the depth of the valley, the height of the mountain, the distant horizon! Nowhere could he be closer to his God, nowhere could he feel His power and might more than when he stood here.
It is to these circumstances that we may owe the fact that Pohanská is perhaps one of the largest enclosed prehistoric settlements in Slovakia, girdled by continuous ramparts.
History

Pohanská was already inhabited in the Neolithic. In various places several polished and flaked stone tools have been found here, lost by the earliest farmers probably while hunting or exploiting timber. The stray finds from the Early Bronze Age – a bronze pin with a pierced head – can be interpreted in a similar way.

The first settlement was not founded until the Late Bronze Age. The people of the Velatice culture built a smaller hillfort here. It was above all the acropolis and some of the terraces, which were evidently already being modified at this time, that were occupied. Insights into the occupation of this period have been provided by pottery finds. Typical of the period were amphora-shaped forms and storage vessels, but also ordinary kitchen ware – pots, plates, bowls and cups. Bronze artefacts, despite the fact that bronze was the basic raw material at that time, are attested by only a few knives, pins and arrowheads. This suggests that it may have been merely a military fortification, from which even evidence of craft activity – otherwise common in this period – is missing.

children.text: The history of Pohanská reached its culmination with the arrival of the Celts. Already at the time of their arrival in Central Europe their society was structured and hierarchically organised. They therefore understood the building of hillforts as a logical necessity. At the same time the Celts were outstanding craftsmen, above all in metalworking, pottery production and the like. These aptitudes were reflected in the fact that, besides being centres of power, the hillforts also became centres of crafts and trade, to which, of course, cult was added. This type of Celtic hillfort we call an oppidum. In the Late La Tène period (roughly in the 2nd century BC) Pohanská too became such an oppidum.
The fortification

The oppidum on Pohanská covered an area of 49 ha. This space was protected by three rings of ramparts. The outer ring formed a kind of semicircle turned to the north-east. The builders followed a similar shape when laying out the middle rampart as well. The acropolis was protected by a third, considerably smaller ring, which followed the course of the contour lines most closely of all.
Štefan Janšák describes the fortification of the hillfort as follows (the designations of the ramparts in the description correspond to his sketch in the image above):

The entrance to the hillfort once led from the eastern side through a gateway that is relatively well preserved to this day. The double ramparts bend into the line of the road so as to form a kind of defensive entrance bastions. The continuous ramparts are the following: the outer g h = 750 m, h i f = 1,250 m; the inner a b c = 850 m, c d = 700 m. The area enclosed by these ramparts is 38.2 ha, overgrown with beech and oak forest. This first part of the hillfort lies on the hillsides of the mountain of Pohanská, around whose foot the ramparts run. Between the entrance to the hillfort and its highest point there is a difference in elevation of 117 m. The flat crown of the mountain, inclined to the east and south-east, is girdled on the north-western, western, southern and south-eastern sides by the rampart s r l o p = 480 m and protected by a parallel entrenchment j k = 300 m. Two radial ramparts, l m = 120 m and l n = 70 m, join the core. In all, then, the length of all the artificially created ramparts is 4,520 m and the outer circuit of the hillfort a b h i e f r a = 2,475 m.

blocks.text: The rampart g h is attached at point g to the steep rock on which the ruin of the historic castle stands, and thus protects the saddle between spot heights 497 and 419 against an incursion from the north-eastern side. The rampart h f bends three times at a right angle at the points i, e, ei and is attached to the steep slope at point f. The rampart j k protects the relatively easy approach from the north-west, both of its ends being attached to rocky, steep spurs. In the same way the rampart a b ends with its point a in steep terrain. The rampart s r l o p protects the summit plateau as the core, or acropolis, of this settlement. At the place p s the approach is barred by a rocky crag. The radial ramparts l m, l n close off the hillfort against a possible approach from the side r f. All the ramparts are very distinct, rising 0.5 to 2.00 m above the terrain. Only in the space between h and i, where cultivated fields extend, do the ramparts disappear, leaving only an insignificant flat swell 10–20 cm high. Access to the hillfort was by the gateway h c. From there one ascended to the acropolis by an artificial, gently rising road c o, in places cut into the rock, which opened into the core of the hillfort at the gateway o.
blocks.author: Štefan Janšák
blocks.source: Niektoré novoobjavené hradiská slovenské (Some Newly Discovered Slovak Hillforts), 1928

blocks.text: A peculiarity of this hillfort are the two springs Pi, P2, situated behind the protective entrenchments. Both made possible a long stay even for a larger number of people and cattle within the protected zone. The spring Pi also served to supply the medieval castle. It retains the remains of good walls, which served to capture it and keep it clean. It was no doubt with the aim of connecting with this spring that the protective rampart was dug through at point b.
blocks.author: Štefan Janšák
blocks.source: Niektoré novoobjavené hradiská slovenské (Some Newly Discovered Slovak Hillforts), 1928

blocks.text: The most interesting part of the hillfort is its core o p s r o. It lies 117 m higher than the gateway h c; on the less steep sides p o r s it is protected by ramparts, from the north-east at the place /; s is a steep rocky crag. The plateau of the summit slopes to the east and south-east (fig. 2), thus setting itself as favourably as possible towards the sun. On its surface lies a thick occupation layer of black humus, in places resembling soot, mixed with a quantity of sherds. There are also funnel-shaped pits there, the largest of which are 15 m in diameter and 5 m deep. French scholarly literature calls these artificial structures „mardely“. About their purpose at Pohanská little can be said without prior digging. Specialists consider them to be communal dwelling pits. In Slovakia they have not so far been identified at a single hillfort.
blocks.author: Štefan Janšák
blocks.source: Niektoré novoobjavené hradiská slovenské (Some Newly Discovered Slovak Hillforts), 1928

children.text: The defensive walls were built of earth and of roughly dressed stones of local sandstone, laid dry in courses to form a facing. The construction was strengthened by massive wooden posts. The Celts in Gaul built their fortifications in a similar way – this was the so-called murus gallicus. From the inner side the fortification was accessible by an earthen bank. The wall-walk was probably protected by wooden crenellations. The height of the fortification without the crenellation can be estimated at about 2.5 m and its width at 4 m. Pavel Dvořák states that at the front there was a wall of stones laid dry (without mortar), and behind it an earthen rampart with a timber construction. At the strategically most vulnerable points stood a double wall, a „murus duplex“ (the earthen rampart was bounded by two walls, the rear one higher than the front one). The architectural high point of Pohanská was the entrance gateway to the acropolis, the highest and separately fortified place. A road broken inwards led up to it, flanked on both sides by a defensive wall. The entrance was closed by solid wooden gates built of thick beams, as a find of a long iron nail shows. Anyone who wished to take the gateway had to attack defenders who pressed in not only from both sides of the broken rampart, but also from a high, massive wooden tower that stood on piers above the gateway. The post that supported it in the middle divided the road to the acropolis into two streams. Only an experienced builder and hundreds of labourers could have erected such an ingenious fortification. The high level of organisation of the society is confirmed by further finds as well, for example five large storage vessels not far from the rampart. They were too big for a single family and must have served for organised supply (at least in time of siege).
Finds

Behind the walls of the oppidum several craft workshops were based and at work. Besides the potters, the most numerous community was formed by the smiths. If we go by the body of finds, they produced agricultural and craft implements, objects of everyday use and even jewellery and brooches. Food producers, traders and, of course, warriors are archaeologically attested. Under the roots of a tree were found a smith’s shovel, axes, a drill, a chisel, a scythe, shears, a hook key and a sword scabbard, all gathered up in haste probably in a smith’s forge (the assemblage contained finished products, semi-finished pieces and also damaged items ready for repair). The second treasure – a hoard (it also contained a heavy anvil) – lay beside a conspicuous boulder with which its unfortunate owner had marked the way to his property. The third hoard contained iron currency bars, which served not only as raw material but also as a primitive means of payment. The hoard also contained iron shackles, evidently as evidence of an organised penal authority, and scales for gold coins as crowning proof of monetary trade. The objects were buried in the ground in the first half of the 1st century BC, and that is probably when Pohanská came to an end.

The oppidum was destroyed by fire, but the more specific reasons – whether it was enemies (the Dacians? Germanic peoples?), the outbreak of a fire through carelessness, or an internal social conflict – could not be traced. In my opinion, however, the buried hoards that their owners never recovered rather suggest that the hillfort fell to an enemy attack. If we are speaking of the middle of the 1st century BC, then we must reckon with the fairly real possibility that the hillfort was destroyed by the Dacians, who in the middle of the 1st century militarily subdued the Celtic population in the territory of present-day Slovakia, weakened as it was by fighting with Rome. The fate of the Celts was decided by a battle not far from Lake Neusiedl, where in the first century BC they suffered a defeat at the hands of the Dacian army led by King Burebista. After this victory the Dacians gradually began to occupy Celtic territory. Its function was probably taken over by the newly emerging oppidum on the site of present-day Bratislava.
